top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz; B027) answers a first-order question about who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand. It pairs a skill-demand and education-technology account with transparent local labour-market designs on import competition. The core work is mature and has been replicated, extended and contested for a decade or more. The critiques have refined the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects without overturning the qualitative finding of slow, geographically concentrated adjustment. The citation should be worded around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, not the task model, to limit overlap with Acemoglu's 2024 prize, and it should avoid effect sizes. Katz anchors the skills strand, so the credited names match what the citation claims. The costs are real: Dorn is excluded, the work may read as two strands joined by Autor, and the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes are adjacent. If the committee narrowed the scope to import competition, Autor, Dorn and Hanson would be the right set. P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) is a clean, mature originator pair, but its quantitative importance is established indirectly and it overlaps partly with the 2022 prize, so I rank it second. A prize for P002 is still better than no award (P000), given its foundational mechanism and nearly thirty years of extension. I have not independently verified any claim.
recusal_note: No tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz (P001) or Kiyotaki and Moore (P002) is apparent from the profile. Disclosed ties, not adjudicated: a 2026 IJIO paper co-authored with chair John Hassler (a P002 supporter) and former chair Tore Ellingsen; marriage to former Swedish prime minister Magdalena Andersson, a public fact with no apparent bearing on any shortlisted candidate; and my empirical-micro and IO orientation, which may lean me toward directly tested evidence.
